newsitem.title: CHILE: El Abra working after accident - Cyprus Amax.
newsitem.headline: El Abra working after accident - Cyprus Amax.

text.p: A serious accident at El Abra copper mine in northern Chile has not paralyzed production at the mine, a spokesman for owners Cyprus Amax Minerals Co said.

The accident, in which four workers died, buried a key conveyor belt carrying copper ore from the mine to the crusher plant, but the mine and the plant continued to work, said spokesman Michael Rounds.
"The mine is not paralyzed," Rounds said by telephone from Cyprus headquarters in Denver. "We have a considerable amount of ore stockpiled, enough to maintain production."
He said officials were evaluating the accident's impact on the mine but that he did not believe any contract commitments would be affected.

Officials at the mine near Calama in northern Chile had said the mine's entire staff had stopped work to join in rescue efforts after a tunnel over the conveyor belt collapsed, burying four workers. They had said normal production could not resume until tonnes of debris had been removed from the conveyor belt.
But Rounds said the mine could maintain production by carrying the ore to the crusher by truck.
He said the mine's heap leaching facilities are largely automated and that they did not stop working during the accident.
"We will still have to dig it out," said Rounds, referring to the conveyor belt, but said there was no word yet on how long that would take.

He believed the tunnel would have to be rebuilt, as it protects the belt as it runs through a steep gorge on the way from the mine to the crusher. "I don't think the reason for having the tunnel has changed," he said.
The accident occurred when the tunnel's steel structure collapsed without warning as workers loaded earth onto it, El Abra said in a statement Wednesday.
Officials at the mine could not be reached for comment Thursday.
The mine made its first cathode in August and is due to reach full production of about 225,000 tonnes of copper a year in 1997.
The mine is owned 51 percent by Cyprus Amax and 49 percent by Chilean state copper company Codelco.
